title: Min-Weight k-Clique hypothesis
formal: Is the following hypothesis true? For every fixed integer \(k\ge3\) and every real \(\varepsilon>0\), there is no uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every simple undirected \(n\)-vertex graph with integer edge weights in \([-n^{100k},n^{100k}]\), outputs a minimum-total-edge-weight \(k\)-clique, or correctly reports that no \(k\)-clique exists, with probability at least \(2/3\), and has worst-case running time \(O(n^{k-\varepsilon})\). The time bound is over both input graphs and all random choices, with \(k\) fixed and \(n\to\infty\). This is the fixed weight-range version of Hypothesis 7 in the cited survey.
why: Weighted clique optimization is a basic way to express interactions among several selected objects. Its conjectured exponent underlies exact-time lower bounds for problems far beyond clique detection. A polynomial exponent improvement would change those conditional barriers, while a proof would establish strong unconditional limits for a family of explicit polynomial-time tasks. The question also separates the difficulty of arbitrary edge costs from that of merely requiring all pairwise adjacencies.
status_note: The survey explicitly poses this fixed-range randomized hypothesis in 2018. Related min-weight clique assumptions continue to be used in ITCS 2026, with different weight-constant quantifiers. A bounded later-work search through 14 September 2026 did not identify a resolution of this exact formulation; conditional reductions and continuing use are not an independent proof of openness.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 2026-09-14; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

progress.text: Vassilevska Williams states the randomized fixed-range Min-Weight k-Clique Hypothesis as Hypothesis 7 on printed page 16, distinguishing it from unweighted and exact-weight hypotheses.

Abboud, Bringmann, Dell and Nederlof’s full version connects falsifying the Orthogonal Vectors conjecture with faster minimum-weight clique and hyperclique algorithms for sufficiently large clique size. This is a conditional implication, not a resolution.

Hu, Nogler and Saha use a related min-weight clique conjecture for lower bounds on dynamic tree edit distance and related problems. Their Conjecture 1 permits the weight exponent constant to depend on the desired fractional saving; it does not replace the fixed exponent 100 in this card.

importance.reason: A core fine-grained hardness hypothesis for weighted optimization that extends the triangle/APSP frontier to every fixed clique size and supports lower bounds across graph, sequence and geometric problems. Its fixed weight range and full randomized model make the barrier broad and testable.

sentences: The task finds a fixed-size clique minimizing the sum of its integer edge weights.
The hypothesis says that no randomized algorithm saves a positive constant from the exponent k for the source’s full polynomial weight range.
Its formal model charges uniform word-RAM computation and requires a correct complete answer with bounded error on every graph.
A resolution would affect the fine-grained foundations of weighted graph, geometric and sequence optimization.
The card preserves the fixed signed range and distinguishes newer conjectures whose weight exponent is quantified differently.

definitions: An instance has an integer \(n\ge k\), labelled vertices \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), a set \(E\subseteq\binom{[n]}2\), and weights \(w:E\to\mathbb Z\) satisfying \(|w(e)|\le n^{100k}\). A feasible answer is a set \(S\in\binom{[n]}k\) with \(\binom S2\subseteq E\); its weight is \(\sum_{e\in\binom S2}w(e)\). Any minimizing set is acceptable, and a special failure symbol is correct exactly when no feasible set exists. The input is a read-only array consisting of \(n\) and, in lexicographic order for all unordered vertex pairs, an adjacency bit, sign bit and unsigned weight magnitude, each in its own word; absent edges use zero sign and magnitude. The output is the sorted list of \(k\) vertex labels or the failure symbol. For each fixed \(k\), an algorithm is one finite program independent of \(n\), using words of \(W=\lceil d\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits for some fixed integer \(d\ge100k+4\). The constant \(d\) may depend on the program and \(k\), but not on \(n\) or the input graph. One operation reads or writes a constant number of addressed words, branches or compares, performs a word-level Boolean operation or shift, adds, subtracts or multiplies modulo \(2^W\), divides unsigned words with quotient and remainder when the divisor is nonzero, or obtains one fresh uniform random \(W\)-bit word. Shifts by at least \(W\) produce zero. All work memory initially contains zero, and arbitrary precomputed tables depending on \(n\) are not supplied. A fixed number of registers, addressing, input reads, all preprocessing and output writes are charged. Random words are mutually independent. There is no real arithmetic, oracle, quantum operation or nonuniform advice. Uniformity is with respect to \(n\); a different finite program is allowed for each fixed \(k\). Formally, the prohibited bound would give constants \(C,n_0\), depending on the program, \(k\) and \(\varepsilon\), such that every run on every valid instance with \(n\ge n_0\) uses at most \(Cn^{k-\varepsilon}\) operations, while the full output is correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on each instance.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the hypothesis with all its quantifiers, or of its negation. A refutation must supply some fixed \(k\ge3\), some \(\varepsilon>0\), and a finite algorithm with a proved \(O(n^{k-\varepsilon})\) worst-case time bound and the stated per-instance success probability for the full weight range. A proof of the hypothesis must exclude every such algorithm for every fixed \(k\ge3\). A conditional reduction from another unproved hypothesis does not prove it unconditionally. Polylogarithmic or other \(n^{o(1)}\) savings, algorithms only for smaller weights or vertex weights, and approximations to the optimum do not refute it. The integer weights and exact combinatorial output define the algorithmic task; this yes/no hypothesis is not a numerical estimation problem with additive tolerance.

context_blocks.text: The source fixes the weight range \([-n^{100k},n^{100k}]\) and asks whether the exponent \(k\) can be decreased by any positive constant. For fixed \(k\), these are polynomially bounded integers with logarithmic bit length, not unbounded-precision real costs. The constant \(100\) is retained from the source rather than replaced by an unspecified polynomial.

The elementary \(O(n^k)\) bound gives a reference scale for fixed \(k\). The hypothesis permits smaller factors such as powers of logarithms: it only excludes a fixed positive saving in the exponent. Consequently, an \(n^{k-o(1)}\) algorithm can coexist with the claim.

Edge weights are essential. The survey distinguishes unweighted clique detection and vertex-weighted clique optimization, whose algorithmic bounds need not match the edge-weighted problem. It also separates minimum weight from the requirement that a clique have total weight exactly zero. These related tasks must not be substituted in the formal statement.

The three-vertex case is closely connected to all-pairs shortest paths through subcubic reductions. Higher clique sizes provide additional hardness assumptions used for sequence alignment, geometric optimization and graph problems across density ranges. This makes the family useful beyond a single graph-search task.

Abboud, Bringmann, Dell and Nederlof establish implications connecting weighted clique hardness to the Orthogonal Vectors conjecture. Such conditional connections strengthen the network of evidence but do not prove the hypothesis. Hu, Nogler and Saha still use a min-weight clique conjecture in ITCS 2026; their nonnegative weight range has a differently quantified exponent constant, so it is recorded as a related formulation rather than asserted to be identical to the fixed range here.
